name: SQL vs NoSQL
intent: Relational (SQL) databases and NoSQL databases organise data differently. Pick the one whose shape matches your data, your queries and how you need to scale.
scenario: An online shop stores customers, orders and the items in each order. Pages show one order with its customer and items; support updates addresses; finance wants totals per customer.
problem: The same data can be stored very differently, and each choice makes some questions cheap and others expensive. Choosing by fashion rather than by access pattern leads to painful joins, duplicated data, or schemas that fight the product.

howItWorks.title: Relational: normalised tables and joins
howItWorks.text: Data is split into tables (customers, orders, order_items) linked by keys, and each fact is stored once. SQL joins them on demand, and a fixed schema, constraints and transactions keep the data consistent.

howItWorks.title: Document stores: whole objects together
howItWorks.text: An order is stored as one document with the customer details and items embedded. One read returns everything for a page, and documents need not share a schema. The cost is duplication: the customer's address is copied into every order.

howItWorks.title: Other NoSQL families
howItWorks.text: Key-value stores give very fast lookups by key. Wide-column stores handle huge write volumes across many machines. Graph databases make relationships the first-class citizen. 'NoSQL' is a group of different tools, not one thing.

howItWorks.title: Scaling behaves differently
howItWorks.text: Relational databases scale up easily and replicate well, but joins and multi-row transactions get hard once data is sharded across machines. Many NoSQL stores were designed to shard from the start, and keep related data in one document so queries touch one machine.

howItWorks.title: The lines are blurring
howItWorks.text: Relational databases now store JSON and scale out, and many NoSQL stores offer transactions and query languages. Choose by your actual needs and by what the specific product guarantees, not by the label.

pros: SQL: flexible ad-hoc queries, joins, aggregations and strong guarantees
SQL: a schema and constraints catch bad data early, and the tooling is mature
NoSQL: flexible schema and fast iteration on changing data
NoSQL: designed to scale out, with reads that touch one document or key
cons: SQL: schema changes and horizontal scaling take planning
SQL: joins across shards are expensive or unsupported
NoSQL: duplicated data means updates fan out and can drift apart
NoSQL: ad-hoc queries and reporting across documents are harder
whenToUse: SQL when data is relational, queries vary, correctness matters and you need transactions: orders, accounts, inventory
Document stores for self-contained objects read and written as a unit: profiles, catalogs, content
Key-value for sessions, caches and counters; wide-column for huge time-series and event streams; graph for relationship-heavy queries
whenNotToUse: Do not choose NoSQL only to avoid designing a schema: the schema moves into your application code
Do not choose SQL if the data is genuinely schemaless and enormous with simple access by key
Do not pick either without listing your top queries first
pitfalls: Modelling relational data in a document store, then simulating joins in application code
Embedding data that changes often (such as a customer's address) in many documents
Assuming a NoSQL store gives you the transactions or consistency you need
Choosing for scale you do not have: one well-tuned SQL database goes a very long way
